lesson.title: Linear Search: Checking Every Door
lesson.summary: Introduces linear search as the straightforward strategy of examining each list element in order until the target is found, and analyzes when this simple approach is efficient enough.
lesson.body:
You already know how to traverse a list, visiting each element in turn with a loop. Linear search takes that exact skill and adds one small but powerful idea: instead of just looking at every element, you compare each one to a target value and stop as soon as you find a match. It's called "linear" because the number of comparisons you might need grows in direct, straight-line proportion to the size of the list ,  search twice as many items, and in the worst case you do twice as much work.

Think of it like looking for your friend's name in an unsorted stack of index cards. You have no shortcuts available, because the cards aren't organized by any rule you can exploit. So you pick up the first card, check the name, and if it's not a match, you set it aside and check the next one. You keep going until either you find the name or you run out of cards. That's the entire mechanism behind linear search: a traversal loop with a comparison and an early exit built in.

Here's what that looks like as an algorithm design problem, which you've already practiced framing. The inputs are a list called data and a value called target. The output should be the index where target lives, or some signal (often -1) meaning it wasn't found at all. The steps are: start at index 0, compare data[0] to target; if they match, return 0 immediately; if not, move to index 1 and repeat; continue until you either find a match or reach the end of the list without one.

Consider a concrete list: data = [42, 17, 8, 91, 3, 56], and you're searching for target = 91. The algorithm checks index 0 (42, no match), index 1 (17, no match), index 2 (8, no match), index 3 (91 ,  match!), and returns 3. That took four comparisons. Now search for target = 3 in the same list: you'd check indices 0 through 4 before finding it at index 4, a total of five comparisons. And if you searched for target = 100, which isn't in the list at all, the algorithm would check all six elements, find no match, and return -1 (or whatever "not found" signal you chose) after the traversal completes. Notice that the number of comparisons depends entirely on where ,  or whether ,  the target appears, which is exactly why this behavior is called linear: the worst case (target absent, or at the very last position) requires checking every single element.

This is where linear search's honesty about cost matters. If your list has 6 elements, worst case is 6 comparisons. If it has 6,000 elements, worst case is 6,000 comparisons. There's no cleverness here, no assumption about the data's order ,  which is precisely linear search's strength and its weakness. It works on any list, sorted or not, because it makes no assumptions at all. But that generality comes at a price: it can't skip ahead or rule out large chunks of the list the way a strategy that assumes sorted order eventually will. For now, the important habit to build is recognizing linear search as the default, always-safe fallback: when you don't know anything special about how your data is arranged, checking every item one at a time is guaranteed to work, even if it isn't always the fastest option available.
